Notes: Year Established basis: earliest documented Jewish presence = Hasmonean takeover of Galilee 'at the end of the second century BCE' (c. -100). Aviam (excavator) states 'the village antedating the Hasmonean conquest was inhabited by a gentile population' (3rd-2nd c. BCE settlement on the summit); a Hasmonean coin in the foundations dates the summit walls to after the Hasmonean takeover. Event: Judaization/new fortified Jewish settlement. No count. (Identification with biblical Jotbah / 732 BCE Assyrian records and the Mishnah's 'walled since Joshua' tradition not used: uncertain/legendary and no Iron Age remains reported by the excavator.)
c. 100 BCE: Alexander Jannaeus brought the fortress under Judean control (per Into His Own site, Rutgers/M. Smith). Event: Hasmonean conquest; start of Jewish town. No count.

1st c. BCE (midpoint -50): under Hasmonean rule the crest of the hill was surrounded by a wall, with a thick double wall with towers on the north side (IAA summary). Presence of fortified Jewish hilltop town; no count.

1st c. CE (midpoint 50), Early Roman houses: plastered stepped pools in two houses identified as ritual baths (mikvehs); over 100 sherds of soft limestone (chalk) cups and bowls; Hasmonean coins still circulating with Nero-era coins 'among the Jewish communities in the Galilee'; a room with frescoes in Second Pompeian style. Indicates a substantial, partly wealthy Jewish town observing purity laws. No count.

Early Roman period (1st c. CE, midpoint 50, c.): a new town wall built on the southern part of the hill expanded the town to some 13 acres (c. 50 dunams); mikva'ot found in some houses (IAA summary). Presence of an enlarged Jewish town; no count.
66 CE (start of Great Revolt): Josephus (War 2.20.6 / 2.573) 'built walls in proper places about Jotapata' among the Galilean towns he fortified. Literary attestation of the Jewish town; no count.

Modern scholarly estimate (Mordechai Aviam, excavator, New Encyclopedia of Archaeological Excavations in the Holy Land): 'According to the size of the site, the population of Yodfat can be estimated to have been approximately 1,500-2,000' (midpoint 1750; method: site area within walls c. 12.5 acres). Total population of a Jewish town per the source, on the eve of the 67 CE siege. Same source: if some 5,000 refugees fled in from neighbouring villages there may have been around 7,000 people at the start of the siege (refugee-inflated, not residents; not used).

Modern assessments cited by Wikipedia: estimated population of c. 7,000 on the eve of the siege (Aviam 2002 p. 131; Rogers 2022 p. 229) - includes refugees, so not resident population; Josephus' 40,000 dead contrasted with modern estimate of c. 2,000 killed and 1,200 women and infants captured (Rogers 2022). Casualty/captive figures, Population blank.

Ancient figures (Josephus, War 3.7.36 / 3.337): those slain in the capture and in earlier battles counted at 40,000; 1,200 captives (women and infants). Death toll and captives including refugees and fighters; regarded by modern scholars as inflated. Population blank.
Event: Jotapata taken after the 47-day siege 'in the thirteenth year of the reign of Nero, on the first day of the month Panemus' (Josephus, War 3.339; = c. 20 July 67 CE).

Event: Vespasian ordered the city 'entirely demolished, and all the fortifications burnt down' (Josephus, War 3.338). Destruction of the Jewish town; Population not 0 because captives survived and the source does not state that no Jews remained.

Jewish Encyclopedia (1906, Gottheil & Seligsohn) summarizing Josephus: siege of 47 days; 'Forty thousand of them lost their lives during the siege; and about 1,000 women and children were sold as slaves' (note: Josephus' text gives 1,200 captives). Ancient casualty/captive figures, Population blank.

Destruction 67 CE: town held out 47 days against Vespasian; skeletons of some 30 men, women and children found in a water cistern (IAA summary). Archaeological evidence of the massacre of the inhabitants; no resident count.

c. 68 CE (aftermath): Aviam proposes that 'the bodies of the slaughtered inhabitants of Yodfat were left unburied for over a year' until Jews returned to the town, gathered the bones and buried them in cisterns and caves (one cistern held bones of c. 20 individuals - 12 adults and 8 children - some with trauma). Indicates a brief Jewish return after the destruction; no count.
